Additionally, the outer divertor electron temperature, measured by Langmuir probes, drops below 5 eV (Fig. 2h), and the second peak heat flux commonly associated with RMP-produced lobes is not observed throughout the discharge.

The influence of RMP current and injected gas species on ELM mitigation during partial divertor detachment is systematically examined in Fig. 3. The trends in ELM frequency (fELM, Fig. 3a), ELM-induced energy loss (ΔW/WMHD, Fig. 3b), and inter-ELM peak heat flux (q⊥, Fig. 3c) on the outer divertor target are presented as functions of the applied n = 3 RMP current. In the absence of RMP and detachment, the plasma exhibits natural type-I ELMs at ~35 Hz with energy losses of ~4.5% and a peak divertor heat flux of q⊥ = 1.8 MW/m2. Pure D2 puffing without RMP (IRMP = 0) induces partial ELM mitigation, increasing fELM to 80 Hz while reducing ΔW/WMHD to 2.4% and q⊥ to ~1 MW/m2. Interestingly, D2 puffing alone leads to mixed ELMs with increased ELM frequency before detachment and transiting to lower frequency pure type-I ELMs during detachment. Even parity n = 3 RMP (2–6 kA) further mitigates the ELMs during detachment, raising fELM up to 200 Hz and decreasing ΔW/WMHD to 1%, but no change in q⊥ (1.1 MA/m2). In contrast, N2 seeding—while effective at achieving detachment at lower density and higher temperature—results in weaker ELM mitigation under even parity n = 3 RMP, yielding lower fELM (~50 Hz), higher ELM energy loss (ΔW/WMHD = 3%), and higher q⊥ = 1.3 MW/m2, as seen from the blue star in Fig. 3a–c. The data point for D2 plus N2 seeding under even parity represents discharges with both stationary and nonstationary ELMs (193119 in Fig. 2). Odd parity n = 3 RMP with combined D2 and N2 fueling show to be the most effective approach to achieve detachment with small ELMs, marking more than eight- and four-times reduction compared to natural ELMs, respectively. The ELM energy loss ΔW/WMHD is about 0.3–0.5% as shown in Fig. 3b (also Fig. 2f), while the uncertainty for energy loss calculated from fast equilibrium is large due to the low amplitude. This value is close to the expected requirement for ITER small ELM44, i.e., 0.15% for 15 MA, or 0.3% for 7.5 MA, which are to avoid monoblock (MB) top surface and toroidal gap edge melting, though a detailed evaluation and assessment for the ELM energy fluence is required and dedicated for future exploration study.

The concurrent realization of divertor detachment and RMP-mitigated small-ELM regime is underpinned by several synergistic mechanisms, illustrated in Fig. 2, or the following sections. Crucially, RMPs reduce the required gas fueling rate and density inside the separatrix for detachment onset, namely detachment facilitation, while also lowering the heat flux to the divertor. The resulting small ELMs are not merely a mitigation of large ELMs or RMP-driven small ELMs at high density attached condition30,33, but represent a stable, high-frequency small ELMs regime achieved under the partially detached conditions that are essential for a reactor. In turn, gas puffing suppresses the secondary peak heat flux typically induced by RMPs. This specific combination of a high-frequency small-ELM regime with high confinement (H98 > 1) at a relatively low q95, all within a detached divertor, is a crucial finding. It demonstrates a concrete pathway to integrating core performance with divertor survivability, directly addressing a key challenge for ITER. These interactions are explored in detail in the following sections.

Divertor detachment facilitation by RMP
To systematically document the impact of RMP on the dynamics of the detachment process, dedicated experiments are conducted by employing pure D2 puffing with a gradually increasing rate. This methodology allows us to probe the edge plasma response across a continuous range of densities, which is essential for identifying the underlying physics mechanism that would be impossible to capture with an abrupt gas puffing. Figure 4a–f shows a representative comparison demonstrating how n = 3 RMP facilitates divertor detachment in DIII-D. The discharges analyzed are #193106 (without RMP) and #193107 (with 4 kA even parity n = 3 RMP). This gradually increasing gas puffing prevents abrupt changes in density and ELM dynamics, and the gas puffing waveform is identical for both cases. Even parity n = 3 RMP is turned on earlier when the density is lower, based on the comparable density pump-out with odd parity as introduced in Fig. 2.

In discharge #193106, D2 puffing begins at t = 2 s (Fig. 4a), steadily raising the upper divertor neutral pressure (Fig. 4a) and plasma density (Fig. 4e) and increasing the ELM frequency up to ~130 Hz (Fig. 4b). The core radiation gradually increases from 1 to 1.6 MW, and the power across the separatrix (Psep, Fig. 4c) slightly decreases. Partial divertor detachment is observed at t = 4.4 s, indicated by a sharp drop (~30 ms) in the divertor electron temperature Te,div to below 5 eV (Fig. 4d, blue dashed line) and a jump in the divertor neutral pressure Pdiv. In the experiments, we have found that the divertor detachment happens at a very short timescale (~30 ms) as indicated in the Te,div evolution, which is much shorter than the energy confinement time (~150 ms). At this onset, the D2 puffing rate is ΦD2 = 6.71 × 1021 s−1, with a normalized pedestal density of fG = 0.48 (ratio of pedestal density to Greenwald limit density). Following detachment, the ELM frequency decreases to 80 Hz, and the core radiation power increases to ~2.5 MW.

Discharge #193107 is identical in setup to #193106 except for the application of n = 3 RMP with 4 kA current beginning at t = 2 s (Fig. 4a). The RMP initially induces a density pump-out and ELM mitigation, as reflected in the pedestal density (ne,ped) and Dα emission (Fig. 4e and b). The applied RMP also leads to higher core radiation power compared to #193106. Partial detachment occurs earlier at t = 4.2 s, with a reduced puffing rate of ΦD2 = 6 × 1021 s−1 and fG = 0.4—approximately 11% and 17% lower than in #193106, respectively. While the power across the separatrix (Psep in Fig. 4c) at the time of detachment onset is the same as #193106 within measurement uncertainty, indicating earlier detachment is not due to lower Psep. Notably, RMP results in a lower separatrix density but higher upstream SOL density at ψN = 1.04 across both attached and detached phases from 3.2 to 5 s (Fig. 4f, detailed profile evolution in Supplementary Fig. 2). During detachment, the ELM frequency increases significantly to ~200 Hz, in contrast to the decreasing trend seen in #193106. Despite these differences, the core radiation power during detachment is similar to that in #193106.

A parametric scan of RMP current from 2 to 6 kA reveals a clear correlation between RMP and detachment facilitation. This RMP current scan enables comparison of edge profiles at different RMP amplitudes, allowing us to assess the impact of magnetic perturbations on detachment onset with similar fueling and heating conditions. Figure 4g, h show TS measurements of electron density and temperature profiles at the detachment onset for various RMP current levels. Compared to #193106, increasing RMP current causes a more pronounced density pump-out, yielding lower density inside the separatrix, but higher SOL density (Fig. 4g). This increased SOL density from TS is also consistently observed in the reflectometry (Fig. 4i), which has 80° difference in the 3D phase space compared to TS location, which mean this raised SOL density is not toroidally localized as observed in ASDEX-Upgrade66 tokamak during RMP ELM suppression. Crucially, it is well understood that this raised upstream SOL density aids in divertor detachment by enhanced impurity radiation and momentum loss67,68. Concurrently, the pedestal-top temperature rises by 20–40% (Fig. 4h). This scan clearly demonstrates, for the first time, enhanced radial transport from the pedestal to the SOL induced by RMP during detached conditions, providing systematic evidence that supports earlier, limited observations55.

Figure 4i, j summarizes the dependence of detachment onset density and D2 gas puffing rate on the RMP current. With RMP in the range of 2–6 kA, the line-averaged density at detachment onset drops by 10–30%, pedestal density by 10–15%, separatrix density by 10–20%, while the SOL density at ψN = 1.04 increases by 30–110% from both TS and reflectometry. This pronounced density redistribution is consistent with enhanced particle transport, though a contribution from the modified recycling due to 3D magnetic topology cannot be ruled out. Correspondingly, the required gas puffing rate ΦD2 decreases by ~10% for IRMP = 2–4 kA. However, at higher RMP current (5–6 kA), the required puffing rate approaches that of #193106. Similarly, the reduction in detachment onset density becomes saturated from the pedestal to the core region for IRMP ≥ 4 kA.

Further analysis reveals that the non-monotonic dependence of ΦD2 on RMP current arises because an overly strong RMP has counterproductive outcomes. While it successfully exhausts more thermal particles—lowering the detachment onset density—this effect also demands more fueling and degrades the degree of detachment (DoD)67. The stronger particle exhaust is evident from the increased density pump-out and a more degraded plasma performance (βN falls from 2.2 at 4 kA to 1.8 at 6 kA). Consequently, this greater thermal particle loss requires more fueling to achieve detachment. Furthermore, the stronger RMP leads to a lower DoD67, which decreases from 5 (without RMP) to 3.8 at 4 kA RMP, and falls below 3 above 5 kA RMP, as shown in Fig. 4j—a trend mirrored by the divertor neutral pressure. For moderate RMP currents (2–4 kA), the lower DoD is attributed to a lower extrapolated ion flux at a reduced core density (Fig. 4i), as the measured ion and heat fluxes are lower than reference discharge #193106.

In summary, moderate RMPs facilitate detachment by enhancing particle transport: this reduces the density inside the separatrix while raising it in the SOL, thereby lowering the gas puffing for detachment. However, an overly strong RMP degrades this effect, ultimately reducing the DoD even though the detachment onset density is lower. This finding is supported by comparable experiments in the EAST tokamak (Supplementary Fig. 3), which also showed a reduction in detachment onset density with n = 1 RMP and pulsed Neon seeding, though a similar reduction in the impurity puffing rate was not confirmed.

2D and 3D simulations show consistent detachment facilitation and heat flux mitigation by RMP
SOLPS-ITER simulations with a two-dimensional (2D) boundary qualitatively reproduce the experimental observations by incorporating RMP-enhanced transport effects. These simulations compute the background plasma by solving the 2D Braginskii equations, while the neutral distribution is calculated using a kinetic neutral transport code. Turbulence-driven radial transport is represented through ad-hoc cross-field transport coefficient profiles. Neoclassical transport effects are not included, as all relevant particle drifts (E×B, B×∇B) are activated in the modeling. The cross-field particle and thermal diffusivities are iteratively tuned to match TS measurements of electron density and temperature profiles at the LFS midplane. Figure 5a, b present the SOLPS-ITER derived particle (D⊥) and thermal (χe) diffusivity profiles for #193106 without RMP and #193108 with 5 kA RMP at the time of detachment onset (see Fig. 4g, h). A noticeable increase in both cross-field particle diffusivity (D⊥) and thermal diffusivity (χe) is observed around the separatrix for the RMP case. Specifically, the elevated χe in the region 0.98 < ψN < 1 is a direct consequence of the flattened temperature gradient there. This finding aligns with the established understanding that RMP-driven magnetic islands near the separatrix act to flatten (not shown in Fig. 4h) the local Te profile38. For discharge #193108, a reduction in stored energy indicates that ~0.5 MW of additional power is exhausted to the SOL due to the applied RMP. In the simulations, the separatrix density at the LFS midplane is scanned to determine the detachment threshold for both RMP and non-RMP cases. By incorporating the transport coefficients from Fig. 5a, b, and the additional 0.5 MW of SOL power for the RMP case, SOLPS-ITER simulations predict the detachment onset density, shown in Fig. 5c as Jsat versus ne,sep. The stars denote the threshold ne,sep required to achieve detachment, defined by a target electron temperature below 10 eV. Comparing discharges #193106 and #193108, the simulations predict a 19% reduction in the detachment onset density due to RMP, in good agreement with the 21% reduction observed experimentally. These simulations again confirm that the RMP-induced enhancement in the cross-field transport helps to increase the SOL density and facilitate detachment by enabling more efficient plasma cooling.

EMC3-EIRENE simulations with a fully 3D boundary geometry support the experimental findings described above. EMC3-EIRENE69,70 solves a coupled set of fluid equations for plasma particle, parallel momentum, and energy, along with kinetic neutral particle transport for a 3D magnetic field configuration. The magnetic perturbation field, comprising both vacuum and plasma response, is calculated using the MARS-F71 code and superimposed on the 2D axisymmetric equilibrium field from discharge #193022 (Fig. 4g, h) to form the magnetic geometry for EMC3-EIRENE. The plasma backgrounds from EMC3-EIRENE are used as inputs for the ERO2.072,73 simulations, which self-consistently account for the carbon impurity erosion, transport, and radiation. These simulations are conducted with 4 MW of power in the SOL region, using constant cross-field diffusivities (D⊥,D = D⊥,C = 0.3 m2s−1, χi = χe = 1 m2s−1), in accordance with Fig. 5a, b at the separatrix. The use of constant coefficients is a standard and practical approach for these 3D simulations, chosen to ensure numerical stability and convergence. This assumption allows us to qualitatively isolate the effect of the RMP itself without the added complexity of spatially varying transport. A deuterium plasma with primary carbon impurity content is assumed, and a 4% carbon erosion yield is adopted based on SOLPS-ITER modeling for DIII-D74. The D2 puffing rate and the RMP current are scanned to qualitatively compare with the features observed in the experiment.

Figure 6a shows the simulated LFS midplane electron density profiles for IRMP = 0, 4, and 6 kA, using a D2 gas puffing rate of ΦD2 = 6.4 × 1021 s−1, which is insufficient to trigger detachment for these three cases. Comparing to the case without RMP, simulations with 4 and 6 kA RMP exhibit reduced density inside the separatrix (pump-out) and increased SOL density, the higher RMP current lead to stronger SOL density enhancement—highlighting the role of RMP in enhancing cross-field transport. Additionally, the simulations show toroidal variations in the SOL density caused by 3D effects, while the overall SOL density remains substantially higher than in the no-RMP case. These results qualitatively agree with experimental TS measurements shown in Fig. 4g, although it should be noted that the linear plasma response model used here does not include the nonlinear RMP penetration effects at the pedestal-foot38,75.

Figure 6b, c show the simulated heat flux on the outer divertor target for the case without RMP and IRMP = 6 kA, respectively, with a higher D2 gas puffing rate of ΦD2 = 7.7 × 1021 s−1 to sustain detachment. At the outer target, the case without RMP remains marginal to detach, with still high enough target heat flux and Te,div near 10 eV (Fig. 6b). The application of 6 kA RMP leads to partial detachment, with strongly mitigated target heat flux and a maximum Te,div of ~2 eV (Fig. 6c). These simulations again align well with the experimental results in Fig. 4, affirming the beneficial impact of RMP enhanced cross-field transport on divertor detachment.

Revisiting LSN divertor experimental results46 reinforces the observation that effective RMP-induced transport enhancement (density pump-out) facilitates detachment (Supplementary Fig. 4). The key involves activating RMP at lower density to trigger magnetic island38,76 and increase turbulence transport66,77 at the plasma edge, thereby inducing density pump-out. This is notably more difficult to achieve at higher density in both tokamak38,75 and stellarator78. Together, these experimental and numerical results suggest that RMP-facilitated detachment is a general phenomenon, contingent on the ability of RMP to effectively enhance edge plasma transport.

RMP mitigates heat flux during detachment without second heat flux peak
In addition to facilitating detachment, both experimental data and EMC3-EIRENE simulations reveal further benefits from combining RMP with divertor detachment. Figure 6d shows the simulated heat flux on the outer divertor target under attached conditions with 6 kA RMP and a low D2 puffing rate (ΦD2 = 1.3 × 1020 s−1). A distinct secondary peak in heat flux appears alongside the primary peak, a known concern for ITER when integrating RMP-based ELM control with detachment54. However, EMC3-EIRENE simulations demonstrate that this secondary peak disappears once the gas puffing rate is increased sufficiently to achieve detachment, as shown in Fig. 6c. This suppression of the secondary peak is corroborated by DIII-D experiment. Langmuir probe measurements of the outer divertor target heat flux for discharge #193106 (without RMP) and #193108 (5 kA RMP) are presented in Fig. 6e, f, respectively. In #193108, a secondary peak appears around 2 s, decreasing progressively with increasing gas puffing and plasma density (see Fig. 4a–f). This peak vanishes entirely at approximately 3 s—well earlier than the onset of detachment—and this trend is consistently observed in all discharges with applied RMP. Contrary to our observations, in the ASDEX-Upgrade experiments51, the lobes disappeared only under strong detachment.

Another notable effect is the further reduction of the primary heat flux during detachment when RMP is applied. As shown in Fig. 6c (with RMP), the peak heat flux is significantly weaker compared to the case without RMP in Fig. 6b. Experimental results reinforce this finding: during detachment, the primary heat flux drops by more than a factor of two with RMP (Fig. 6f vs. Fig. 6e). In #193106 (without RMP), the peak shifts outward and reduces to ~2 MW/m² after detachment onset. In contrast, #193108 (5 kA RMP) sees further mitigation of the peak to below 1 MW/m², attributed to increased SOL density. These findings underscore the role of RMP in not only aiding detachment but also mitigating heat loads on the divertor.

RMPs are known to generate magnetic island chains near the separatrix, which overlap to form magnetic stochasticity38 and lobe structures79 at the plasma edge. Figure 7a illustrates the perturbed magnetic topology caused by RMP in DIII-D discharge #193022 under both attached and detached conditions. The MARS-F80 and FLARE54 codes are used to compute the linear plasma response and field line tracing, respectively, revealing 2–3% edge stochasticity and lobes within ψN = 0.98–1. These 3D structures induce a 3D distribution of edge plasma parameters81 and enhance radial and parallel transport at the plasma edge38,54, thereby facilitating divertor detachment. The resulting edge 3D plasma distribution is evident in the CIII emission simulated by the EMC3-EIRENE, as shown in Fig. 7b, where lobe structures are prominent in the attached condition but vanish during detachment. Notably, since the E×B drift effect is not included in the EMC3-EIRENE simulations, detachment in the inner divertor is weaker than in the outer divertor, as evident by relatively stronger CIII emission and a target temperature of around 6 eV.

Experimentally, the existence of these lobes is confirmed by CIII impurity emission imaging. Figure 7c presents the 2D distribution of CIII emission from a tangential camera (TTV) at the same toroidal location and time as the simulations in Fig. 7a. Bright emission peaks, marked by arrows, appear on the HFS in both attached and detached phases, aligning with the ψN = 1 flux surface from the simulation (red curves). The TTV observation is consistent with the EMC3-EIRENE simulation during the attached condition but differs during detachment, which is likely because the detachment in the simulation is deeper compared to the experiment (partial detachment). During detachment, the peak impurity emission at the outer divertor target diminishes, while the X-point emission remains prominent. This behavior reflects target cooling and a redistribution of radiative losses, with a relatively enhanced role near the X-point. While the MHD model predicts lobe structures on both the HFS and LFS, experimental CIII emission shows pronounced lobes on the HFS only. On the outer divertor leg, lobes are not clearly visible due to the limited viewing angle of the TTV camera.

Decreasing RMP response in detached plasma
Simultaneous full RMP ELM suppression and detachment remain elusive in DIII-D experiments due to significantly reduced plasma response in high collisionality plasma. Previous modeling showed reduced plasma response at higher collisionality in attached plasmas.

Figure 8a shows the derived profiles of edge bootstrap current density for DIII-D discharge #193108 from low to high density/pedestal collisionality. Discharge #193108, as shown in Fig. 4g and h, was performed with increased RMP current (5 kA) under otherwise similar conditions to discharge #193106. Compared to low pedestal collisionality (υ*e ≈ 0.2), it exhibits over a 50% reduction in pedestal bootstrap current during high collisionality detached conditions. The degraded pedestal gradient at high collisionality is thought to be caused by the electron temperature gradient (ETG) mode82. The edge kink response, essential for ELM suppression, is thought to be amplified by the edge pedestal bootstrap current83. Therefore, a substantial decrease in the plasma response is anticipated with a significant reduction in the edge bootstrap current, as illustrated in Fig. 8b for the HFS poloidal magnetic response calculated by the ideal MHD code GPEC84. Here, the phase difference between the upper and lower row coil currents is performed, and the poloidal magnetic perturbation at the HFS midplane is shown because of its crucial role in ELM suppression85,86. Figure 8b reveals more than a 70% decrease in the HFS magnetic response with increased pedestal collisionality from υ*e ≈ 0.2 to 1.8. Nonlinear two-fluid MHD simulations via the TM1 code38 predict over 15 kA RMP current for full ELM suppression in detached plasma, surpassing the capability of 3D systems in DIII-D (maximum 6 kA). Additionally, Fig. 8b highlights a continuous ~40° phase shift for maximum HFS magnetic response, underscoring the importance of 3D configuration optimization with changing pedestal conditions87.

Figure 8c–e displays the radial magnetic response, denoted as δBr, on the plasma control surface for RMP in even parity with υ*e ≈ 0.2 (Fig. 8c), and both even (Fig. 8d) and odd (Fig. 8e) parity for detached conditions with υ*e ≈ 1.8. For υ*e ≈ 0.2 and even parity RMP (Fig. 8c), the patterns in δBr align well with the field line pitch depicted by the black curves, indicating effective resonance of the applied RMP with the plasma edge. However, for υ*e ≈ 1.8 and even parity RMP (Fig. 8d), the magnetic field strongly decreases and misaligns with the field line pitch at the LFS midplane. For υ*e ≈ 1.8 and odd parity RMP (Fig. 8e), the magnetic response still aligns with the field line pitch, although the amplitude is significantly reduced. Additionally, the magnetic response with components resonating at the pedestal-top is stronger for odd parity compared to even parity, consistent with observations in Fig. 2 that odd parity RMP leads to stronger ELM mitigation. These observations and analysis underscore the sensitivity of plasma response with plasma collisionality86, particularly the change in the pedestal structure when transiting from attached to detached divertor.

## Methods

DIII-D tokamak
DIII-D91 National Fusion Facility is a tokamak research device operated by General Atomics in San Diego, California, for the U.S. Department of Energy. DIII-D is the largest magnetic fusion research facility in the U.S. The DIII-D program is pioneering the science and innovative technology that will enable the development of nuclear fusion as the next-generation energy source. The discharges presented in this paper have the major and minor radius of 1.7 and 0.6 m, respectively, the toroidal magnetic field Bt = 1.7 T at the magnetic axis, the plasma current Ip = 1.27 MA, 6 MW heating power, and 4.5 Nm torque are injected by using the neutral beam injection (NBI), edge safety factor q95 = 3.5, βN = 2-3, H98 = 1.1–1.3. DIII-D is equipped with two sets of 3D coils: one is the ex-vessel coils, consisting of 6 saddle coils at the low field side midplane called C-coils, and another one is the in-vessel coils, consisting of 12 saddle coils with an upper and lower row of 6 coils called I-coils. In our experiments, the C-coils are used to compensate the n = 1 intrinsic error field, and the I-coils are used to generate n = 3 RMP with the upper row and lower row coil current controlled separately.

EAST tokamak
The Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (EAST)2 is a superconducting tokamak magnetic fusion energy facility constructed and operated by the Institute of Plasma Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, in Hefei, China. EAST is aiming to conduct fundamental physics and engineering research on advanced tokamak fusion reactors with a steady, safe, and high-performance, to provide a scientific base for experimental reactor design and construction, and to promote the development of plasma physics and related disciplines and technologies. The referenced discharge has the plasma major radius of 1.85 m, minor radius of 0.45 m, and the toroidal magnetic field Bt = 2.25 T at the magnetic axis, the plasma current Ip = 0.45 MA with q95 ~ 5.2, βN = 1.6, H98 = 1 heated by 1.3 MW from the lower hybrid wave and 1.3 MW from NBI. The divertors in EAST have been upgraded to full tungsten. EAST equips 16 in-vessel saddle coils with an upper and lower row of 8 coils each. In our experiments, the 3D coils are used to generate n = 1 RMP with the upper row and lower row coil current controlled separately.

Diagnostics for kinetic profile and divertor parameters
In DIII-D, the profiles of electron temperature and density from the core to the SOL are measured by the multi-pulsed high-resolution Thomson Scattering system92,93. The profiles of ion temperature, the carbon density, and rotation are measured by the charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy system94 for C6+ particles. To obtain well-resolved profiles, the data are averaged over 100 ms within 70–95% of the ELM period. The pedestal height is obtained from hyperbolic tangent fits with edge profiles. The heat flux on the upper divertor target is measured by one tangential camera of the fast infrared television camera (IRTV), and the peak heat flux on the outer divertor target is derived from the IRTV data. The tangential TV viewing of the upper divertor is used to measure the C3+ and N2+ impurity emission. In both DIII-D and EAST, an array of Langmuir probes mounted on the divertor target is used to measure plasma parameters on the divertor target, including the heat flux, ion saturation current, and electron temperature.

Kinetic equilibrium reconstruction
By using the OMFIT integrated modeling framework95, a multi-step workflow is used to add pressure and plasma current density constraints in the equilibrium reconstruction to improve the accuracy of the reconstructed equilibrium. The workflow (for one iteration) includes three parts: profile fitting based on the existing equilibrium, power balance calculation for total pressure and plasma current components, and equilibrium reconstruction with pressure and current density constraints. Usually, two or three iterations would be sufficient to produce high-quality equilibria for a transport study. In the power balance part, NUBEAM96 is used for NBI-driven current and fast ion pressure calculation, and bootstrap current is derived from the measured pressure profiles based on the Sauter model65. Then TRANSP97 is employed to create the total pressure by combining thermal pressure and fast ion pressure together, and provide total plasma current density by considering external driven current, bootstrap current, and calculated Ohmic current by solving poloidal field diffusion. The equilibrium reconstruction part is performed by the EFIT98 code.

Determination of divertor detachment
Divertor detachment is accompanied by an abrupt drop of the target temperature to below 5–10 eV, and a roll-over in the ion saturation current measured by Langmuir probes, an abrupt increase in the neutral pressure measured by a pressure gauge, and radiation power moves towards the X-point measured by a bolometer. All these indications are consistently observed in DIII-D by other diagnostics, including bolometer and tangential TV. In EAST, the indications from Langmuir probes are used to determine the onset of detachment. The degree of detachment (DoD) is defined as the ratio between the extrapolated target ion flux (obtained by scaling with core density) and the measured ion flux at the divertor target. A commonly used formula67 is

DoD = Γtarget,extrapolated / Γtarget,measured

where Γtarget,extrapolated is target ion flux expected from attached scaling using core line-averaged density, Γtarget,measured is the ion flux measured by Langmuir probes at the divertor target. In the experiment, the ion flux near the outer strike point (separatrix) is used to derive DoD. Usually, 2 < DoDpeak < 10 is thought of as partial detachment.

Uncertainty and error bar definition
The error bars presented in this study represent different sources of uncertainty depending on the measurement type. Specifically, for the electron density of the separatrix (ne,sep) in Fig. 2h, as well as ne,ped, ne,sep and ne,sol in Fig. 4f measured by Thomson scattering (TS), the error bars reflect the systematic uncertainties associated with the diagnostic system itself93. In contrast, the error bars shown in Figs. 3, 4g–j, and 5a, b originate from statistical uncertainties due to time averaging of the measured data. These distinctions are maintained to accurately represent the nature of the uncertainty in each dataset.

SOLPS-ITER simulation
Drift-dependent modeling of the experimental discharges was performed for a better understanding of the physics involved, using the state-of-the-art boundary plasma code package, SOLPS-ITER99, the coupled version of the 2D multi-fluid transport code B2.5100, and the 3D kinetic neutral transport code EIRENE101. The B2.5 fluid code computes the background plasma by solving the 2D Braginskii equations and provides the solutions to EIRENE. Then EIRENE computes and returns the source and sink terms for plasma particles, momentum, and energy due to plasma-neutral interactions. The simulations were carried out for a deuterium (D) plasma with carbon (C) wall and targets. Simulated particles in the modeling include ions (D+, C+, C+2, C+3, C+4, C+5, C+6), atoms (D, C) and molecules (D2). A complete set of atomic and molecular reactions is accounted for in the modeling, including neutral-neutral collisions. All particle drifts, E×B, B×∇B, viscosity, and the associated currents are activated in the modeling.

EMC3-EIRENE simulation
EMC3-EIRENE is a numerical code used to model the plasma boundary. It is a coupling between the plasma fluid code EMC3 and the neutral kinetics EIRENE code. EMC369 is a Monte Carlo 3D plasma fluid code that solves a set of reduced Braginskii fluid equations for particles, parallel momentum, and energies for electrons and ions. The code models parallel electron and ion heat conductivity using classical assumptions. Perpendicular transport is determined by coefficients for anomalous particle transport (D⊥) and anomalous electron and ion heat transport (χ⊥), which are free model parameters. EIRENE101 is a kinetic edge transport code that solves the transport equations for neutral atoms and molecules, accounting for collisional processes. The code calculates ionization sources, momentum sources/losses, and energy sources/losses due to atomic/molecular processes, such as charge exchange and ionization. EMC3-EIRENE models impurity transport using a fluid approach, causing energy losses to the main plasma through excitation and ionization. The trace fluid approach assumes that impurities only cause small density perturbations and impact the main plasma species through ionization and excitation via an energy loss term in the energy balance equation.

Plasma response calculation
GPEC code84 is used to calculate the ideal MHD perturbed equilibrium and the magnetic perturbations. For a given kinetic equilibrium and 3D coil configuration, GPEC calculates perturbatively the total (vacuum plus ideal MHD kink response) 3D magnetic response of the plasma to the 3D coils in full toroidal shape geometry. In this paper, the poloidal magnetic perturbation at the HFS midplane is used to quantify the change of magnetic response according to previous studies85,86. The MARS-F code71 is used to calculate the magnetic perturbations generated by 3D coils. It solves the single fluid, perturbed MHD equations in full toroidal geometry.

Key results: For ITER, having an external “control” knob that would enable us to suppress ELMs while maintaining a stably
attached divertor in Q=10 operation with a high-collisionality pedestal bottom and low-collisionality pedestal top is indeed
attractive. It is possible, these results contribute to the development of such a tool set, but there is insufficient information to
assess if this is indeed the case, or if the observations are a slightly new variation on previously observed phenomena. The
Reviewer suspects that while there is good material here for a Nuclear Fusion paper, the results are not sufficiently novel for
a Nature Communication. Detailed comments are given below.

Rather, the meaning of “facilitation” used here appears to be a different one. It is used in reference to the value of the
pedestal (or core) density at the time of detachment. Typically, detachment is achieved at higher pedestal Greenwald

### Reviewer 3

The present manuscript addresses a relevant topic in the fusion community, i.e. the relation between plasma detachment,
mandatory to ensure plasma facing components survivability, and Resonant Magnetic Perturbation, which is the chosen
strategy for ITER in order to mitigate the deleterious Edge Localised Modes. In principle the authors are claiming that the use
of RMPs indeed facilitate the access to detachment, which is achieved at lower density according to their claims.
Furthermore other advantages arises because of the use of RMP during detached states, as improvement of confinement
during detachment, enhanced heat flux mitigation, absence of a second heat flux peak, andsimultaneous achievement of
small ELMs with partial divertor detachment. They claims to have evidences of the aforementioned processes coming from 2
different devices, DIII-D and EAST.
I want to clarify that the data presented by the authors are actually relevant and interesting but despite effort I do not think that
the conclusion derived are sufficiently robustly supported for being published in such a prestigious journal. In the following
the list of my main concerns supporting this conclusion. They are not provided in priority
ordering but just
1. One the my main concern regards the conclusion derived from Figure 2. According to the authors the use of the RMP
facilitate detachment and this in their opinion shown by noticing that detachment is achieved at lower density showing in this
respect the central density as a reference. Actually this is to me not appropriate for several reason: first of all RMP
application are know to cause a different density peaking and this is associated as well to the process of pump out. A more
robust support to the conclusion of the authors would have been derived by showing that detachment is achieved at lower
separatrix density. This point is partially answered in Figure 3 where the authors claims that separatrix density at
detachment onset is reduced by 10-20%. This is a very delicate question given the uncertainty on the separatrix localisation
in presence of RMPs (with induced magnetic bulging caused by magnetic stochasticity because of perturbed magnetic field).
The authors uses kinetic equilibrium reconstruction to infer separatrix position, but w/o accounting for any 3D effect as
caused by RMP. This uncertainity in the separatrix position needs to be considered together the error bars of the density
estimate shown in Fig 3 (according to which the separatrix density w/o RMPs is within 1 sigma compatible with the value
with maximum density pumpout). Therefore I don't think the authors are in the position of claiming that detachment is
occurring at lower separatrix density with RMPs, which is the relevant figure of merit to be considered as far as exhaust
physic is concerned. I would also like to noticed that the different peaking in presence or absence of RMP is seen also from
Figure 3 given that the ratio ne_core/ne_sep is not constant
2. Still on Figure 3 I think that the example shown for EAST are rather peculiar: the authors attribute the detachment
achievements to Ne seeding. Actually detachment is achieved approximately after 0.5s from the second Neon puffing.
According to recent models [Henderson et al IAEA 2023] this time is in the same ball-park of Ne resident time in the diveror
region and therefore it would be questionable attributing detachment as caused by impurity injection. Also in this case it is
not possible to deduce the separatrix condition (ne_sep, Psep or Te_sep) with or w/o RMPs and therefore we can't state
unambiguously that detachment is facilitated by RMP applocation.
3. To support their claim according to which RMP application are facilitating detachment onset, the authors performed a
series of SOLPS-ITER simulations with drift-activated. Actually as shown in literature (e.g. Brida NME 2019, Rea NF 2015),
the SOL profiles with applied 3D magnetic perturbation are intrinsically 3D and therefore it is not clear which profiles are
taken as reference for constraining SOLPS simulations. I do find the use of a 2D code for a clear 3D geometrical problem not
appropriate and therefore I don't think the results of SOLPS are really promoting the claims of the author: they simply
confirm that with increased radial transport easier detachment is achieved (since at similar Psep this will be clearly associated to
broader target heat profile thus easier to be detached)
4. It is actually quite difficult to interpret Fig 6 (a) concerning the DIII-D part. Indeed while it is clearly observed a
perpendicular heat flux decrease at OSP, there is a simultaneous increase of the flux in a different radial position still of the
order of 1.5 MW/m^2. It is difficult to intepret this as a signature of partial detachment. I think that the comparison of the radial
profiles of main quantities (ne, Te, jsat) might reveal features which are not addressed and considered in the present paper.
But this is not clearly a reference case scenario to be compared with RMP cases
5. Also when comparing even and odd parity the authors does not provide information on the possible difference of
detachment onset relevant quantities like ne_sep or Psep between the two different configuration. Any inference of better
performances of one configuration w.r.t. to the other would not be possible w/o essential exhaust relevant information
6. As a minor point, in the introduction the authors made a comment on ITER operation claiming that ITER is expected to
operate at relatively high density for divertor detachment with [...]. This is actually inaccurate, since ITER is indeed foreseen to
operate at high gas throughput (i.e. high neutral pressure) but this is not impacting the plasma density achieved since
plasma fuelling is ensured by Pellet operation. On the other side the chosen strategy for ensuring plasma detachment in
ITER is a combination of high gas throughput and impurity seeding [see Pitts, Nucl. Mat. Energy 2019].
In conclusion I don't think the authors provide enough clear clearer evidences of the real benefit in term of detachment accessibility
facilitated by application of RMPs. As stated to me detachment onset are occurring within the experimental uncertainty at the
same separatrix parameters (ne_sep, te_sep). No information are provided in terms of power crossing the separatrix and
only information about core density are claimed as important, which is partially inappropriate. The use of a 2D transport code
with respect to an inherent 3D problem is to me of limited use. Therefore I don't think that the paper is adequate for a
publication in such a prestigious journal
